title: She Spoke Without Meaning Offence
intro: In al-Anbari’s account, Abu Qays returns from fighting with the Aws so altered in appearance that his wife has to hear his voice before she knows him. He answers her surprise by describing what he has carried for Banu Malik, from his coat of mail to the responsibilities of command. The twenty-four verses in the Mufaddaliyyat follow him out on his travelling camel and end with a reflection on how little even a well-equipped man can foresee.

translation: She spoke without meaning anything unseemly.
“Wait. Now your voice has reached me.”
1.sharh: The wife has drawn back from the stranger at her door. Her first words here ask for a moment. Hearing him speak has given her what looking at him could not.

translation: You did not know him when you studied him.
War is a ghoul with pains of its own.
2.sharh: He calls himself “him”, seeing the unfamiliar man from his wife’s side of the door. The ghoul of folk belief can change shape, and war has worked a change on his.

translation: Whoever tastes war finds its flavour
bitter. It pens him on hard ground.
3.sharh: War reaches the body twice, in the taste left in the mouth and in the patch of ground on which a man must lie.

translation: My helmet has rubbed my head bare. I taste
no sleep beyond a snatched doze.
4.sharh: The helmet has left a mark she can see. His sleep has been worn just as thin, broken into dozes between duties.

translation: I work for the greater part of Banu Malik.
Every man works at his own concern.
5.sharh: What took him away from home was a whole clan’s business. He treats their affairs as his own everyday obligation.

translation: I have laid by for my enemies a woven coat of mail,
ample as a pool spread over a plain.
6.sharh: The metal links make a flexible surface. Seen across the body, the ample coat catches the light like a sheet of still water.

translation: I hold it up off me with a gleaming blade,
an Indian sword, white as salt and keen.
7.sharh: The long skirt of mail needs support. Al-Asma'i understood the line as referring to its being hitched to the sword’s scabbard. Salt supplies the image for the blade’s clean white sheen.

translation: A trusty cutting blade with a biting edge,
and a curved brown shield that takes the blows.
8.sharh: The first half finishes the description of the sword. The brown curve beside it is a leather shield, completing the figure with two differently coloured surfaces.

translation: The gear of a man ready to stake his life, watchful
against time, tough and slow to panic.
9.sharh: All that equipment belongs to one man. Readiness to risk his life coexists with a watchfulness that comes from knowing what fortune can do.

translation: Resolve and strength are better than
giving way, feebleness and fright.
10.sharh: The weight of the equipment has been visible. Now he sets out the steadiness of judgement it takes to carry responsibility for others.

translation: A sandgrouse is one thing, its chick another,
nor is the one tended like the herdsman among men.
11.sharh: The Arabic word for the chick is a little version of the adult bird’s name. The shepherd image adds a distinction in responsibility to the distinction in age.

translation: We do not flinch at loss of life. We repay
our enemies measure for equal measure.
12.sharh: He borrows the language of the grain measure. The same vessel that measured what his people suffered measures out what their opponents receive.

translation: We drive them back with a force in full career,
with chiefs at its head and men who push them back.
13.sharh: A group in motion takes shape around its leaders. The word for chiefs also evokes prominent noses, giving the force a face and a front.

translation: They are like lions beside their cubs,
growling in thickets and bends of the valley.
14.sharh: The lions have cubs beside them. Their growling has a particular cause, guarding the vulnerable creatures in their keeping.

translation: Until it clears, and there is our standard
amid a company of men all of one kin.
15.sharh: As battle clears, one can see the banner and the men gathered round it. In his account they belong together long before they assemble to fight.

translation: You could have asked the horsemen, when war gathered up its skirts,
how slow I was, and how quick.
16.sharh: The horsemen were witnesses when the battle gathered pace. He invites his wife to hear from them exactly when he held back and when he hurried forward.

translation: Do I share the wealth that I love
among them, and answer the caller’s cry?
17.sharh: Generosity has a cost because the wealth matters to its owner. His neighbours can judge him by what he gives as well as by how he answers a call.

translation: I strike the helmet crest on the day of battle
with my sword, my arm reaching far enough.
18.sharh: At the opening his own helmet had rubbed his head bare. The matching object here is the crest on another man’s helmet, within reach of his arm.

translation: I cross a waste where death is feared,
riding a pale, eager she-camel.
19.sharh: His duties take him beyond the reach of the other horsemen. The pale camel gives him the means to cross open country alone.

translation: She has many gaits and the build of a bull camel,
furnished with Hiran gear and saddle cloths.
20.sharh: The comparison to a male camel conveys her strength. The cloth from al-Hira introduces colour and workmanship into a portrait that began with movement.

translation: She gives her pace despite fatigue and runs clear of
the goad, sure-footed and free of a limp.
21.sharh: She can still offer speed late in the journey. Her rider trusts the steadiness of her stride enough to give her her head.

translation: The edges of her saddle pads seem
caught in a scouring, gusting north wind.
22.sharh: The flying corners make a wind visible. They might be whipping about in a northerly gale, so fast is the motion of the mount beneath them.

translation: I dress the saddle with a patterned covering
from al-Hira, or one pieced from strips.
23.sharh: The rider chooses the covering. It may carry a woven design or a pattern made by joining separate pieces of cloth.

translation: On her I see my business through. A man
is held in pledge to a two-faced trickster.
24.sharh: The journey is within his power to make. Its outcome still belongs to time, pictured as a keeper of pledges who can show either of two faces.

1.1.4-5.head: قيل الخَنا
1.1.4-5.meaning: “Speaking basely”, saying something offensive or unseemly.

1.2.4.head: إِسماع
1.2.4.meaning: Hearing. His voice has reached her and supplied the recognition.

2.1.3.head: تَوَسَّمَ
2.1.3.meaning: To scrutinise someone’s features for signs of identity.

2.2.2.head: غول
2.2.2.meaning: Ghul, a destructive being in old tales said to change its shape.

3.2.3.head: جَعجاع
3.2.3.meaning: Hard, inhospitable ground, or a narrow place of confinement.

4.1.2.head: حَصَّ
4.1.2.meaning: To rub hair away, leaving a bare patch.

4.1.3.head: البَيضَة
4.1.3.meaning: A helmet, named after its rounded shape.

4.2.4.head: تَهجاع
4.2.4.meaning: A brief doze or snatch of sleep.

5.1.3.head: جُلّ
5.1.3.meaning: The greater part or main body.

5.1.4-5.head: بَنو مالِك
5.1.4-5.meaning: Banu Malik, his people among the descendants of Malik of the Aws in Yathrib.

6.1.3.head: مَوضونَة
6.1.3.meaning: A coat of mail made from closely interlinked rings.

6.2.3.head: القاع
6.2.3.meaning: A level stretch of ground over which water spreads.

7.1.1.head: حَفَزَ
7.1.1.meaning: To push up or hold off, here the long skirt of mail.

7.1.3-4.head: ذو رَونَق
7.1.3-4.meaning: “One of bright sheen”, a sword named by its polish.

7.2.1.head: مُهَنَّد
7.2.1.meaning: An Indian blade, a name associated with fine sword steel.

8.1.3.head: وادِق
8.1.3.meaning: A quality of the edge, variously understood as biting, piercing or eager for blood.

8.2.1.head: مُجنَأ
8.2.1.meaning: A convex shield, curving around its bearer.

9.1.1.head: بَزّ
9.1.1.meaning: A man’s equipment, including his arms and clothing.

9.1.3.head: مُستَبسِل
9.1.3.meaning: One prepared to hazard his life.

9.2.4.head: مِجزاع
9.2.4.meaning: Someone quick to panic or give way to distress.

10.2.1.head: الإِدهان
10.2.1.meaning: Giving way or temporising when firmness is called for.

10.2.3.head: الهاع
10.2.3.meaning: Timidity or fright in the face of difficulty.

11.1.2.head: قَطا
11.1.2.meaning: Sandgrouse, desert birds that travel to water in flocks.

11.1.4.head: قُطَيّ
11.1.4.meaning: A diminutive of the name for sandgrouse, here its chick.

11.2.1.head: المَرعِيّ
11.2.1.meaning: One in another’s care. The image extends the idea of tending a flock to human leadership.

12.2.2-4.head: كَيل الصّاع بِالصّاع
12.2.2-4.meaning: “Measure for measure”. A sa' is a traditional measure of grain.

13.1.3.head: مُستَنَّة
13.1.3.meaning: A troop sweeping forward at speed.

13.2.2.head: عَرانين
13.2.2.meaning: Prominent noses, figuratively the chiefs who lead a people.

13.2.3.head: دُفّاع
13.2.3.meaning: A forceful repulse, or the men who deliver it.

14.2.1.head: نَهَتَ
14.2.1.meaning: To growl or give a deep sound from the chest.

14.2.3.head: غيل
14.2.3.meaning: Dense cover or a thicket where lions shelter.

14.2.4.head: أَجزاع
14.2.4.meaning: The bends or sides of a valley.

15.1.4.head: غايَة
15.1.4.meaning: A standard by which a fighting group can be recognised.

15.2.5.head: جُمّاع
15.2.5.meaning: A gathering drawn from different lineages.

16.1.3.head: الخَيل
16.1.3.meaning: The horses, standing here for the riders who witnessed the fighting.

16.1.5.head: قَلَّصَ
16.1.5.meaning: To gather up one’s skirts. Here battle is personified as drawing itself up for action.

17.2.3-4.head: دَعوَة الدّاعي
17.2.3-4.meaning: “The caller’s call”, the appeal of someone seeking help.

18.1.2.head: القَونَس
18.1.2.meaning: The crest or upper part of a helmet.

18.1.4.meaning: The din of battle, then battle itself.

18.2.5.head: باع
18.2.5.meaning: The reach of the outstretched arms.

19.1.2.head: الخَرق
19.1.2.meaning: An open waste hard to cross.

20.1.2.head: أَساهيج
20.1.2.meaning: The different gaits of a camel.

20.1.3.head: جُمالِيَّة
20.1.3.meaning: A she-camel with the powerful build of a male.

20.2.2.head: حارِيّ
20.2.2.meaning: Hiran, referring to saddle furnishing from the Iraqi city of al-Hira.

20.2.3.head: أَقطاع
20.2.3.meaning: Pieces of cloth or leather used as saddle furnishings.

22.1.3.head: وَلِيّات
22.1.3.meaning: Saddle pads lying next to the camel’s back.

22.2.3-4.head: حَصّاء زَعزاع
22.2.3-4.meaning: A gale that strips things bare and shakes them.

23.1.3.head: مَعقومَة
23.1.3.meaning: A closely woven covering with a patterned design.

24.2.2-3.head: ذو لَونَين
24.2.2-3.meaning: “The one with two colours”, time in its favourable and adverse aspects.
